items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "allele"?
options: A thread-like structure of DNA, carrying genetic information in the form of genes.
An alternative form of a gene.
The X and Y chromosomes, which determine sex: XX female, XY male.
The transmission of genetic information from generation to generation.
items.answer: An alternative form of a gene.
items.markingKey: Allele: an alternative form of a gene.

items.stem: Explain why the proportion of boys and girls born is approximately equal.
items.answer: Half of sperm carry X and half carry Y; all eggs carry X; fertilisation is random, so there is a 1:1 ratio of XX and XY.
items.markingKey: sperm X or Y in equal numbers [1]; eggs all X [1]; random fertilisation [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why siblings with the same parents can look different.
items.answer: Each inherits a different combination of alleles from each parent, because gametes differ (meiosis) and fertilisation is random.

items.stem: Draw a genetic diagram to show how sex is inherited in humans, and state the probability that a child will be female.
items.answer: XX × XY → gametes X, X / X, Y → XX, XX, XY, XY → probability female = 0.5 (50%).
items.markingKey: parents [1]; gametes [1]; offspring and 50% [1] [3]

items.stem: A couple already have 4 daughters. Use a genetic diagram to explain the probability that their next child will be a boy.
items.answer: Parents XX × XY; gametes X, X and X, Y; offspring XX, XX, XY, XY; probability of a boy = 0.5 (50%), regardless of previous children.
items.markingKey: parental genotypes [1]; gametes [1]; offspring [1]; 50% and independent of previous births [1] [4]

items.stem: A genetic counsellor in Accra uses a karyotype (a picture of all the chromosomes from one cell) to explain inheritance to a family. (a) State the number of chromosomes in a normal human body cell and how many pairs this is. (b) Explain how you could tell from the karyotype whether the person is male or female.
items.answer: (a) 46; 23 pairs. (b) Look at the sex chromosomes: XX female, XY male (Y is much smaller).

items.stem: What is the chance that a human baby will be a boy?
items.markingKey: Mother gives X; father gives X or Y with equal probability.

items.stem: Explain how a gene controls a characteristic such as eye colour.
items.answer: The gene codes for a protein (e.g. an enzyme making pigment); different alleles code for different versions of the protein, giving different colours.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "mRNA"?
options: The structure in the cytoplasm where amino acids are joined to make a protein.
A sequence of three bases that codes for one amino acid.
The sequence of bases in DNA, in which each set of three bases codes for one amino acid.
A messenger molecule that carries a copy of the base sequence of a gene from the nucleus to the ribosome.
items.answer: A messenger molecule that carries a copy of the base sequence of a gene from the nucleus to the ribosome.
items.markingKey: mRNA: a messenger molecule that carries a copy of the base sequence of a gene from the nucleus to the ribosome.

items.stem: Explain how the sequence of bases in a gene determines the shape of a protein.
items.answer: Each triplet codes for an amino acid, so the base sequence determines the order of amino acids; the order determines how the chain folds and so the shape and function of the protein.
items.markingKey: triplets → amino acids [1]; order of amino acids [1]; folding / shape [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how a change in one base of a gene could affect an enzyme.
items.answer: It may change one amino acid, altering the folding and the shape of the active site so that the substrate no longer fits.

items.stem: A protein contains 400 amino acids. Calculate the minimum number of bases in the gene that codes for it, and explain your answer.
items.answer: 1200 bases
items.markingKey: 3 bases per amino acid [1]; 400 × 3 = 1200 [1] [2]

items.stem: A protein contains 700 amino acids. Calculate the minimum number of bases in the gene that codes for it, and explain your answer.
items.answer: 2100 bases
items.markingKey: 3 bases per amino acid [1]; 700 × 3 = 2100 [1] [2]

items.stem: A cell in the human body produces amylase. The gene for this protein is on one of the chromosomes in the nucleus. (a) Explain why the order of amino acids is important. (b) Explain why a mutation in the gene could prevent the protein working.
items.answer: (a) It determines how the protein folds and its shape, so whether it can carry out its function. (b) Changed base sequence → different amino acid(s) → different shape (e.g. active site / binding site) → no longer functions.

items.stem: Explain why a nerve cell and a muscle cell from the same person contain the same genes but different proteins.
items.answer: Only some genes are expressed in each cell type, depending on the cell's function.

items.stem: A gene contains 600 bases that code for a protein. How many amino acids are in the protein?
items.markingKey: 3 bases per amino acid: 600 ÷ 3 = 200.

items.stem: Which term is defined as "an unspecialised cell that divides by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised"?
items.answer: Stem cell
items.markingKey: Stem cell: an unspecialised cell that divides by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised.

items.stem: Explain why gametes must be haploid.
items.answer: So that when two gametes fuse at fertilisation the zygote has the diploid number; otherwise the chromosome number would double each generation.

items.stem: Explain why cells produced by meiosis are genetically different.
items.answer: Chromosome pairs separate randomly (independent assortment), giving different combinations of alleles in each gamete.

items.stem: A maize cell with 20 chromosomes divides by mitosis. How many chromosomes are in each daughter cell?
items.markingKey: Mitosis keeps the number: 20.

items.stem: Each body cell of a chimpanzee contains 48 chromosomes. (a) State the number of chromosomes in a gamete nucleus and in a zygote. (b) A single cell divides by mitosis every 24 hours. Calculate the number of cells after 72 hours and the total number of chromosomes in all those cells.
items.answer: (a) gamete 24; zygote 48 (b) 8 cells; 384 chromosomes

items.stem: Each body cell of a rice plant contains 24 chromosomes. (a) State the number of chromosomes in a gamete nucleus and in a zygote. (b) A single cell divides by mitosis every 20 hours. Calculate the number of cells after 60 hours and the total number of chromosomes in all those cells.
items.answer: (a) gamete 12; zygote 24 (b) 8 cells; 192 chromosomes

items.stem: A scientist studies cell division in a chicken, which has 78 chromosomes in each body cell. (a) State the number of chromosomes in a cell produced by mitosis and in a cell produced by meiosis. (b) Explain the importance of meiosis in sexual reproduction.
items.answer: (a) mitosis 78; meiosis 39 (b) Halves chromosome number so the zygote is diploid; produces variation in gametes.

items.stem: A scientist studies cell division in a pea, which has 14 chromosomes in each body cell. (a) Explain why the cells produced by mitosis are genetically identical. (b) Explain the importance of meiosis in sexual reproduction. (c) State where meiosis happens in a flowering plant and in a mammal.
items.answer: (a) Chromosomes are copied exactly before division and one copy of each goes into each new cell. (b) Halves chromosome number so the zygote is diploid; produces variation in gametes. (c) Plant: anthers and ovules / ovaries. Mammal: testes and ovaries.

items.stem: What is the name for "nuclear division giving rise to genetically identical cells"?
items.answer: Mitosis
items.markingKey: Mitosis: nuclear division giving rise to genetically identical cells.

items.stem: Each body cell of a maize plant contains 20 chromosomes. (a) State the number of chromosomes in a gamete nucleus and in a zygote. (b) A single cell divides by mitosis every 20 hours. Calculate the number of cells after 80 hours and the total number of chromosomes in all those cells.
items.answer: (a) gamete 10; zygote 20 (b) 16 cells; 320 chromosomes

items.stem: A scientist studies cell division in a pea, which has 14 chromosomes in each body cell. (a) Explain why the cells produced by mitosis are genetically identical. (b) State where meiosis happens in a flowering plant and in a mammal. (c) Describe the role of stem cells.
items.answer: (a) Chromosomes are copied exactly before division and one copy of each goes into each new cell. (b) Plant: anthers and ovules / ovaries. Mammal: testes and ovaries. (c) Unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis and can become specialised to replace or repair tissues.

items.stem: What is the name for "the observable features of an organism"?
items.answer: Phenotype
items.markingKey: Phenotype: the observable features of an organism.

items.stem: Explain why two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child (brown is dominant).
items.answer: Both parents are heterozygous (Bb); each passes on the recessive allele b; the child is bb.
items.markingKey: both heterozygous [1]; each passes recessive allele [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a genetic diagram gives only the probability of offspring phenotypes.
items.answer: Fertilisation is random, so which gametes fuse is a matter of chance; actual numbers vary, especially with few offspring.

items.stem: In humans, cystic fibrosis is controlled by one gene. The allele for no cystic fibrosis (F) is dominant to the allele for cystic fibrosis (f). A cross is made between parents with genotypes FF and ff. (a) State the phenotypes of the parents. (b) Draw a genetic diagram (Punnett square) to show the possible genotypes of the offspring. (c) State the expected ratio of phenotypes.
items.answer: (a) no cystic fibrosis and cystic fibrosis (b) gametes F and f; offspring all Ff (c) all no cystic fibrosis
items.markingKey: (a) both phenotypes [1] (b) gametes [1]; offspring genotypes Ff, Ff, Ff, Ff [1] (c) ratio [1] [4]

items.stem: A breeder has a pea plant showing tall and wants to know its genotype. It is crossed with one showing dwarf. The offspring are 40 with tall and 0 with dwarf. (a) State the genotype of the parent with dwarf. (b) Deduce the genotype of the parent with tall. Explain your answer using a genetic diagram.
items.answer: (a) tt (b) TT: all offspring show tall; if it were Tt about half would be dwarf. TT × tt → all Tt.
items.markingKey: (a) tt [1] (b) correct genotype [1]; reasoning [1]; genetic diagram with gametes and offspring [1] [4]

items.stem: In tomato plants, stem colour is controlled by one gene. The allele for purple stems (P) is dominant to the allele for green stems (p). A cross is made between parents with genotypes PP and pp. (a) State the phenotypes of the parents. (b) Draw a genetic diagram (Punnett square) to show the possible genotypes of the offspring. (c) State the expected ratio of phenotypes. (d) The cross produced 40 offspring. Calculate the expected number with green stems.
items.answer: (a) purple stems and green stems (b) gametes P and p; offspring all Pp (c) all purple stems (d) 0
items.markingKey: (a) both phenotypes [1] (b) gametes [1]; offspring genotypes Pp, Pp, Pp, Pp [1] (c) ratio [1] (d) 0/4 × 40 = 0 [1] [5]

items.stem: Two parents both have tall but their first child has dwarf. In pea plants the allele for tall (T) is dominant to the allele for dwarf (t). (a) Deduce the genotypes of the parents and explain. (b) Explain why the actual number of children with each phenotype in a family may differ from the expected ratio.
items.answer: (a) Both Tt: the child is tt, so each parent must carry t; they show tall, so they must also have T. (b) Each fertilisation is a random, independent event; with small numbers chance has a big effect.

items.stem: Two parents both have yellow petals but their first child has orange petals. In sunflowers the allele for yellow petals (Y) is dominant to the allele for orange petals (y). (a) Draw a genetic diagram to show the probability that their next child will also have this phenotype. (b) Explain why the actual number of children with each phenotype in a family may differ from the expected ratio.
items.answer: (a) Yy × Yy → YY, Yy, Yy, yy; probability orange petals = 1/4 (25%). (b) Each fertilisation is a random, independent event; with small numbers chance has a big effect.
items.markingKey: (a) gametes [1]; offspring [1]; probability [1] [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Explain why the observed ratio in a cross of 40 offspring may not be exactly 3 : 1.
items.answer: Fertilisation is random; with small samples chance causes deviation from the expected ratio.

items.stem: Two parents both have no cystic fibrosis but their first child has cystic fibrosis. In humans the allele for no cystic fibrosis (F) is dominant to the allele for cystic fibrosis (f). (a) Deduce the genotypes of the parents and explain. (b) State the probability that a child with no cystic fibrosis from these parents is heterozygous. (c) Explain why the actual number of children with each phenotype in a family may differ from the expected ratio.
items.answer: (a) Both Ff: the child is ff, so each parent must carry f; they show no cystic fibrosis, so they must also have F. (b) 2/3 (c) Each fertilisation is a random, independent event; with small numbers chance has a big effect.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 2 of the 3 dominant-phenotype genotypes are heterozygous [1] [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "ABO blood group"?
options: A feature in which the gene responsible is located on a sex chromosome, making it more common in one sex.
A sex-linked condition caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome.
A characteristic controlled by three alleles, IA, IB and Io, in which IA and IB are codominant and Io is recessive.
A situation in which both alleles in heterozygous organisms contribute to the phenotype.
items.answer: A characteristic controlled by three alleles, IA, IB and Io, in which IA and IB are codominant and Io is recessive.
items.markingKey: ABO blood group: a characteristic controlled by three alleles, IA, IB and Io, in which IA and IB are codominant and Io is recessive.

items.stem: Explain why a man cannot pass colour blindness to his son.
items.answer: The son receives the Y chromosome from his father; the colour-blindness allele is on the X chromosome.

items.stem: Explain why blood group O is described as recessive.
items.answer: The Io allele is only expressed when no IA or IB allele is present (IoIo).

items.stem: A mother has genotype IAIA and a father has genotype IAIo. (a) State the blood groups of the parents. (b) Draw a genetic diagram to show the possible genotypes and blood groups of their children. (c) State the probability of a child having each blood group.
items.answer: (a) A and A (b) IAIA (A), IAIo (A), IAIA (A), IAIo (A) (c) A: 100%
items.markingKey: (a) both [1] (b) gametes [1]; four genotypes [1] (c) probabilities [1] [4]

items.stem: A mother has genotype IoIo and a father has genotype IoIo. (a) State the blood groups of the parents. (b) Draw a genetic diagram to show the possible genotypes and blood groups of their children. (c) State the probability of a child having each blood group.
items.answer: (a) O and O (b) IoIo (O), IoIo (O), IoIo (O), IoIo (O) (c) O: 100%
items.markingKey: (a) both [1] (b) gametes [1]; four genotypes [1] (c) probabilities [1] [4]

items.stem: A hospital in Colombo records the blood groups of a family. The mother is group A, the father is group B, and their first child is group O. (a) Deduce the genotypes of the parents, explaining your answer. (b) Explain what is meant by codominance, using this example.
items.answer: (a) Mother IAIo and father IBIo, because the child (IoIo) must have received Io from each parent. (b) IA and IB both contribute to the phenotype in a heterozygote, giving blood group AB.

items.stem: Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A woman with genotype XHXH has children with a man with genotype XHY. Draw a genetic diagram and state the probability that a son will have haemophilia.
items.answer: Gametes XH, XH and XH, Y; children XHXH (unaffected daughter), XHY (unaffected son), XHXH (unaffected daughter), XHY (unaffected son); probability that a son is affected = 0%.
items.markingKey: parental gametes [1]; four offspring genotypes [1]; phenotypes [1]; probability for sons [1] [4]

items.stem: In cattle, the alleles CR (red) and CW (white) are codominant; heterozygotes are roan. A roan parent (CRCW) is crossed with a roan parent (CRCW). Draw a genetic diagram and state the expected ratio of phenotypes in the offspring.
items.answer: Offspring CRCR, CRCW, CWCR, CWCW; 1 red : 2 roan : 1 white
items.markingKey: gametes [1]; offspring genotypes [1]; phenotype ratio [1] [3]

items.stem: Which parent determines the sex of a human child?
options: Neither, it is random in the zygote
items.answer: The father
items.markingKey: Sperm carry either X or Y; eggs always carry X.

items.stem: Hana says: "The mother determines whether a baby is a boy or a girl." Explain whether Hana is correct.
items.answer: The father determines sex: sperm carry either X or Y.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: The father determines sex: sperm carry either X or Y. [2]

items.stem: A dog body cell contains 78 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in one of its gametes?
items.markingKey: Gametes are haploid: 78 ÷ 2 = 39.

items.stem: A genetic counsellor in Colombo uses a karyotype (a picture of all the chromosomes from one cell) to explain inheritance to a family. (a) State the number of chromosomes in a normal human body cell and how many pairs this is. (b) Distinguish between the terms gene and allele. items.answer: (a) 46; 23 pairs. (b) A gene is a length of DNA coding for a protein; alleles are alternative forms of a gene. (c) One chromosome comes from each parent, and the parents may have different alleles of the same gene.

items.stem: Where are proteins assembled in a cell?
items.answer: On ribosomes in the cytoplasm

items.stem: State what is meant by the term stem cell.
items.answer: An unspecialised cell that divides by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised.

items.stem: Explain why cancer can result from uncontrolled mitosis.
items.answer: Cells divide repeatedly without control, forming a tumour that can invade other tissues.

items.markingKey: Mitosis keeps the number: 78.

items.stem: Using a genetic diagram, explain how two heterozygous parents can produce offspring with the recessive phenotype, and how a test cross can identify a heterozygous individual.
items.answer: Aa × Aa; gametes A, a; offspring AA, Aa, Aa, aa; 1 in 4 aa recessive. Test cross: unknown dominant × aa; if any offspring aa → unknown is Aa; if all dominant (large number) → AA.

items.stem: Arjun says: "Blood group AB is caused by an AB allele." Explain whether Arjun is correct.
items.answer: Blood group AB results from inheriting both codominant alleles, IA and IB.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Blood group AB results from inheriting both codominant alleles, IA and IB. [2]

items.stem: In four o'clock plants, the alleles CR (red) and CW (white) are codominant; heterozygotes are pink. A pink parent (CRCW) is crossed with a pink parent (CRCW). Draw a genetic diagram and state the expected ratio of phenotypes in the offspring.
items.answer: Offspring CRCR, CRCW, CWCR, CWCW; 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
items.markingKey: gametes [1]; offspring genotypes [1]; phenotype ratio [1] [3]

items.stem: In chickens, the alleles CB (black) and CW (white) are codominant; heterozygotes are blue-grey. A black parent (CBCB) is crossed with a white parent (CWCW). Draw a genetic diagram and state the expected ratio of phenotypes in the offspring.
items.answer: Offspring CBCW, CBCW, CBCW, CBCW; 4 blue-grey
